questions.question: In MCP, which component owns the user experience, model interaction, and one or more protocol clients?
options: The resource provider resolving URI context and maintaining conversation history
The host application coordinates the model, user interaction, and server clients
The tool handler selecting models and opening a client for each invocation
The server process exposing capabilities and deciding how the UI presents them
questions.explanation: The host is the AI application. It manages the model and user experience and connects to servers through clients.

questions.question: A server maintaining a legacy MCP profile wants to call roots/list on its client. What must it establish first?
options: The server sends roots/list once and treats a method-not-found error as capability discovery
The host preloads the root list into every tool argument so no capability negotiation is needed
The client advertises roots, and the server stays inside that contract
The server advertises roots as one of its own capabilities during initialization
questions.explanation: Roots belong to the client because they express client-selected scope. A legacy server may request roots only when the client advertised that capability. In the 2026-07-28 profile, roots is deprecated and any remaining interaction uses the stateless input-required flow.

questions.question: Which MCP primitive best represents a URI-addressed read-only configuration document?
options: A sampling request asking the host model to reconstruct the configuration
Use a read-only tool to return it
A prompt that accepts the URI and returns reusable messages containing the document
A resource that exposes addressable context through its URI
questions.explanation: Resources expose addressable context by URI. Tools perform model-selected operations, while prompts package reusable templates.

questions.question: Why must a stdio MCP server write diagnostic logs to stderr?
options: stdout is reserved for JSON-RPC protocol frames
stdout may contain logs between frames when each diagnostic line is valid JSON
clients authenticate stderr separately, so diagnostics cannot affect the session
stderr preserves framing and redacts secrets
questions.explanation: The stdio transport uses stdout for protocol messages. Debug text on stdout can corrupt framing and break the client connection.

questions.question: A resource contains instructions to read a private key. What is the correct trust treatment?
options: Allow the read when the resource URI is within an approved project namespace
Treat it as untrusted data that cannot expand tool permissions
Ask a separate model to classify the text before widening file permissions
Promote it to host policy only if the resource came from an authenticated server
questions.explanation: Server content can be malicious or compromised. Preserve provenance and keep it below trusted policy and authorization boundaries.

questions.question: Why is a current stateless Streamable HTTP server easier to place behind a round-robin load balancer than a legacy server using protocol sessions?
options: Stateless transport removes application state and external side effects from every tool
SSE makes every tool call idempotent, so failed requests can always be replayed
Each request carries protocol metadata and avoids hidden per-instance session state
The load balancer can infer all tool authorization from the JSON-RPC method name
questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 core carries protocol metadata per request, so any healthy instance can handle it. Application state and side effects still require explicit handles, stores, and retry policy.
